extra.display_text:
He pulled the slip from its pin and carried it back to the counter. The clerk took it, glanced at the stamp, and reached for her log without ceremony. "Mossback Warrens, first level. Solo, is it?" She didn't wait long enough for the answer to matter—just wrote his name against the line and dipped the stamp. "Goblins, mostly, on that floor. Scouts and warriors. The Guild posts it often enough that I'll tell you what everyone tells everyone: they're small and stupid, and stupid still kills more greenhorns than clever does. Don't let three of them get around you in the dark." She stamped the slip, and the wax-brown seal took its impression with a soft press. Then she slid it across the counter to him, the contract face up—*Clear Mossback Warrens, Level 1 — 120 copper on confirmation, Adventurers' Guild, Ashbridge*—with the seal plain at the bottom. "That's your proof you took it and your proof when it's done. Bring it back when the level's clear and we settle up here." She was already pulling the next paper toward her. "Warrens are a half day east, off the old quarry track—a moss-grown hill, you can't miss the entrance once you're on it. Entrance is open; anything below the first level is your own affair and your own funeral." She paused, quill hovering, and looked at him once more—the staff, the fresh Novice plate. "Nobody's counting how many times you come back for the same floor. That's the whole trick of dungeons. Go down, kill what you can kill, walk out alive, come back stronger. The ones who forget the last part don't come back at all." Behind him the door opened for a pair of women with crossbow cases slung on their backs, letting in a draft of street noise and the smell of wet stone.

He pulled the slip from its pin and carried it back to the counter. The clerk took it, glanced at the stamp, and reached for her log without ceremony.

"Mossback Warrens, first level. Solo, is it?" She didn't wait long enough for the answer to matter—just wrote his name against the line and dipped the stamp. "Goblins, mostly, on that floor. Scouts and warriors. The Guild posts it often enough that I'll tell you what everyone tells everyone: they're small and stupid, and stupid still kills more greenhorns than clever does. Don't let three of them get around you in the dark."

She stamped the slip, and the wax-brown seal took its impression with a soft press. Then she slid it across the counter to him, the contract face up—*Clear Mossback Warrens, Level 1 — 120 copper on confirmation, Adventurers' Guild, Ashbridge*—with the seal plain at the bottom.

"That's your proof you took it and your proof when it's done. Bring it back when the level's clear and we settle up here." She was already pulling the next paper toward her. "Warrens are a half day east, off the old quarry track—a moss-grown hill, you can't miss the entrance once you're on it. Entrance is open; anything below the first level is your own affair and your own funeral."

She paused, quill hovering, and looked at him once more—the staff, the fresh Novice plate.

"Nobody's counting how many times you come back for the same floor. That's the whole trick of dungeons. Go down, kill what you can kill, walk out alive, come back stronger. The ones who forget the last part don't come back at all."

Behind him the door opened for a pair of women with crossbow cases slung on their backs, letting in a draft of street noise and the smell of wet stone.

The road east out of Ashbridge ran between hedgerows and drainage ditches, wide enough for two carts, hard-packed by years of toll traffic. A quarter mile on, the old quarry track split off from it, narrower and stonier, and the city fell behind into fields and wet grass. The morning was mild and grey. A cart overtook him in the first hour, a woman driving and a boy asleep in the bed of it among sacks of turnips; she gave him the flat look country people gave a staff-carrying young man and was gone at a creaking trot. Somewhere off the track a dog barked itself hoarse. Twice crows lifted out of a hedgerow ahead of him and resettled behind. The ground rose slowly after the second hour, the fields giving way to rougher pasture and then to scrub. He smelled the hill before he saw it clearly—wet earth and old growth, a green, spoiled smell that didn't belong to the thin grass around it. Then the track rounded a shoulder of rock and the hill stood up out of the scrub, and it was as the clerk had said: moss-grown, a low round hump of stone clothed in moss so thick it looked padded, dark green even in the grey light. The entrance was a raw mouth in the hill's southern side—a cut archway of worked stone, older than anything else in sight, its edges worn round. Cold air breathed steadily out of it, carrying that same green smell, stronger here, and something else beneath it: animal musk and old smoke. The grass around the opening was trampled flat and dotted with old fire-scars and a few sun-bleached bones too cracked to name. Someone had driven a stubby iron stake into the ground a few paces from the arch, and from it hung a weathered board with the Guild's crossed blade-and-staff burned into it, the wood silvered by rain. Beyond the archway the light gave out after a few paces, into darkness that the cold air kept moving gently in and out.
